title: Coverage and Continuous Integration knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of “Coverage and Continuous Integration”?
options: Coverage and Continuous Integration means the browser can enforce all permissions without the backend.
Coverage and Continuous Integration removes the need for error handling, accessibility checks and tests.
Coverage and Continuous Integration should be implemented by copying a snippet without checking the Angular version.
Coverage and Continuous Integration helps explain and implement one part of an Angular application; choose the API pattern that matches the behavior and verify it.
questions.answer_key: Coverage and Continuous Integration helps explain and implement one part of an Angular application; choose the API pattern that matches the behavior and verify it.
questions.explanation: Coverage and Continuous Integration is a concept in the supplied Angular curriculum. Its correct application depends on the intended behavior, surrounding context and verification.

questions.prompt: How should a learner work with “Measuring code coverage” in this lesson?
options: Assume “Measuring code coverage” works identically across every Angular major and runtime.
Use “Measuring code coverage” to bypass runtime validation of external or user-provided values.
Connect “Measuring code coverage” to the lesson goal, use a focused example, and validate the behavior in the selected Angular environment.
Treat “Measuring code coverage” as a reason to skip the surrounding application context.
questions.answer_key: Connect “Measuring code coverage” to the lesson goal, use a focused example, and validate the behavior in the selected Angular environment.
questions.explanation: The PDF explicitly lists “Measuring code coverage” under Coverage and Continuous Integration. Anchor it in a small example and check the behavior rather than relying on a memorized phrase.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest verification approach for “Coverage and Continuous Integration”?
options: Ignore a failing test if the component looks correct in one browser.
Run the example in a compatible local Angular workspace, test the expected result and one failure case, and document any version limitation.
Assume an SVG diagram proves the code compiled and passed tests.
Treat a successful client-side render as backend authorization evidence.
questions.answer_key: Run the example in a compatible local Angular workspace, test the expected result and one failure case, and document any version limitation.
questions.explanation: Verification evidence should match the running environment. Static teaching snippets are not compiler output, and frontend checks do not replace backend authorization.
